body:
Why were women's movements varied?

Women's movements in post-Independence India addressed different forms of inequality. Their demands included protection from violence, fair working conditions, economic independence, access to resources and greater participation in public decisions.

Not all women's movements developed in the same way. Some organised working women, some opposed harmful practices within families and communities, and others emerged from struggles over forests and local natural resources.

The Chipko Movement

The Chipko Movement developed in the Garhwal Himalayan region of what was then Uttar Pradesh and is now Uttarakhand. It became widely known during the early 1970s.

Villagers opposed commercial tree-felling when forest policies restricted their access to resources needed for daily life and local livelihoods. In some places, forest resources were made available for commercial purposes while villagers faced restrictions on using similar resources for agricultural tools and other necessities.

The movement became associated with non-violent resistance, especially villagers embracing trees to prevent their felling. This action gave the movement its distinctive name.

Women's participation at Reni

On 26 March 1974, women of Reni village in Chamoli district played an important role in preventing tree-felling. Gaura Devi was among the leaders associated with this action.

For the women involved, forests were connected to fuelwood, fodder, water sources, soil protection and the daily needs of village households. Forest protection was therefore both an environmental and a livelihood demand.

Chipko raised wider questions about who should control local natural resources and how forests should be managed. Women also used the organisational experience of these struggles to raise other community concerns, including alcohol-related problems.

The Anti-Arrack Movement in Andhra Pradesh

Another significant mobilisation took place in Andhra Pradesh in the early 1990s. It became known as the Anti-Arrack Movement.

Arrack refers to a locally produced alcoholic drink. In rural communities, heavy alcohol consumption was associated with loss of household income, indebtedness, domestic violence and disruption of family life.

In Dubagunta village of Nellore district, discussions during an adult literacy programme helped women articulate their experiences and organise opposition to the sale of arrack.

The movement spread across villages and developed into a wider demand for prohibition. Its significance went beyond alcohol policy: it brought domestic violence and women's control over household resources into public political discussion.

SEWA: economic organisation of women in Gujarat

The Self-Employed Women's Association (SEWA) was established in Ahmedabad in 1972 under the leadership of Ela Bhatt.

SEWA organised women working in the informal economy. Such workers include street vendors, home-based producers, manual workers and others whose work may lack the employment protections available in formal workplaces.

SEWA developed as a trade union of self-employed women. Its aims included improving income, working conditions, economic security, access to financial services and collective bargaining strength.

The movement is especially relevant to Gujarat because Ahmedabad was its founding centre. It also illustrates how a women's movement can focus primarily on employment and economic independence rather than prohibition or environmental protection.

How these movements are connected

Chipko, the Anti-Arrack Movement and SEWA addressed different immediate problems. Yet each demonstrated that issues often treated as private or local concerns could become subjects of organised public action.

  • Chipko: Forest protection and community livelihood.
  • Anti-Arrack: Alcohol-related harm, household income and domestic violence.
  • SEWA: Recognition, organisation and economic security of informal women workers.

The movements also expanded women's participation in political and social decision-making outside conventional party organisations.

Prelims focus

  • Chipko developed in the Garhwal region of present-day Uttarakhand.
  • Gaura Devi was associated with the Reni village action of 26 March 1974.
  • Chipko combined environmental protection with local livelihood concerns.
  • The Anti-Arrack Movement was associated with Dubagunta, Nellore district, Andhra Pradesh.
  • SEWA was founded in Ahmedabad in 1972 under Ela Bhatt.
  • Trap: SEWA is a women's trade union, whereas the Anti-Arrack Movement centred on opposition to alcohol sales.

[NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, chapter 7, Rise of Popular Movements, printed pp. 129–130 and 137–139; Uttarakhand Biodiversity Board, Chipko Movement of Garhwal Himalaya, section on Reni, 26 March 1974; Food and Agriculture Organization, Standing Up for Trees: Women's Role in the Chipko Movement, section on Gaura Devi; SEWA Bharat, History of the SEWA Movement, sewabharat.org. Consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Women protecting trees during the Chipko Movement in the Garhwal Himalayas.

pictures.alt: Chipko, Anti-Arrack and SEWA link forest, household and work concerns with women's wider participation in public affairs.

title: Women's Movements, Chipko and the Protection of Everyday Livelihoods

body:
The Sardar Sarovar Project

The Narmada River is an important west-flowing river of central and western India. The river and its tributaries pass through a region closely connected with Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat.

The Sardar Sarovar Project, located in Gujarat, was planned as a major multipurpose river-valley project. Its objectives included:

  • Providing water for irrigation.
  • Supplying drinking water to settlements, including water-scarce areas.
  • Generating hydroelectric power.
  • Supporting agricultural and regional development.

The project was especially important to Gujarat because parts of the State experience recurrent water shortages and uneven rainfall.

Why did opposition emerge?

Large dams can create benefits for people living far from the project site. At the same time, reservoirs can submerge villages, agricultural land and forests near the dam.

People displaced by submergence may lose homes, farmland, community institutions, employment and access to forests or other resources. For Adivasi communities and other rural residents, these losses can include important cultural and social connections to particular places.

Consequently, a dam project raises 2 different questions: whether the project produces important public benefits and whether people bearing its direct costs receive fair treatment and rehabilitation.

The emergence of Narmada Bachao Andolan

The Narmada Bachao Andolan (NBA) emerged as an organised movement around 1988–1989, bringing together local organisations and affected communities. Medha Patkar became one of its prominent leaders.

The movement initially emphasised rehabilitation and resettlement of affected families. It raised questions about:

  • Whether displaced families would receive adequate land, housing and livelihood support.
  • How environmental and social costs were assessed.
  • Whether affected communities had a meaningful voice in decisions.
  • Whether the burdens of development were being distributed fairly.

Over time, sections of the movement also opposed further construction of major dams and questioned the wider model of large-scale development.

The debate in Gujarat

The movement faced substantial opposition from supporters of the Sardar Sarovar Project, particularly in Gujarat. Supporters argued that irrigation, drinking-water supply and electricity generation would benefit large populations, including communities facing water scarcity.

The NBA argued that public benefits should not justify inadequate rehabilitation or the neglect of environmental and social consequences.

The positions were not simply development versus environment. The dispute concerned the benefits of the dam, the losses experienced by affected communities, the adequacy of rehabilitation and the fairness of public decision-making.

Judicial intervention

The dispute reached the Supreme Court. In Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India (2000), the Court permitted the Sardar Sarovar Project to proceed subject to conditions, including requirements concerning rehabilitation and environmental safeguards.

The case illustrates the connection between environmental movements, public development projects and judicial oversight.

How does NBA differ from Chipko?

Chipko focused initially on commercial tree-felling, forest access and local livelihoods in the Garhwal Himalayas. Narmada Bachao Andolan focused on large dam projects, displacement, rehabilitation and environmental effects in the Narmada Valley.

Both movements raised concerns about the relationship between natural resources and local communities, but their immediate causes and principal demands were different.

Prelims focus

  • The Sardar Sarovar Project is associated with the Narmada River and Gujarat.
  • The project has irrigation, drinking-water and hydroelectric objectives.
  • Narmada Bachao Andolan emerged as an organised movement around 1988–1989.
  • Medha Patkar is a prominent leader associated with NBA.
  • The Supreme Court permitted project construction subject to safeguards in its 2000 judgment.
  • Trap: Chipko and NBA are both environmental movements, but they developed around different immediate issues.

[NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, chapter 7, Rise of Popular Movements, printed pp. 140–142; Supreme Court of India, Narmada Bachao Andolan v. Union of India, judgment dated 18 October 2000, sections concerning relief, rehabilitation and environmental safeguards; Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Limited, Project at a Glance, ssnnl.org. Consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The different benefits and burdens associated with a large dam project.

title: Narmada Bachao Andolan: Development, Displacement and the Gujarat Connection

body:
Why did linguistic demands arise after Independence?

India contains communities speaking many different languages. After Independence, people in several regions demanded States in which their own language would be widely used in administration, education and political life.

A linguistic State is a State organised substantially around a major regional language. Its creation does not mean that every resident speaks only that language or that linguistic minorities cease to exist.

The linguistic reorganisation of States was an important way of accommodating regional identity within the Indian Union.

Andhra and the beginning of linguistic reorganisation

Telugu-speaking people demanded a separate State from the predominantly Tamil-speaking areas of the former Madras State.

Potti Sriramulu undertook a fast in support of the demand and died in December 1952. The resulting public mobilisation increased pressure on the Union government.

Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953. Its creation became an important precedent for wider State reorganisation.

The States Reorganisation Commission and Act

The Union government appointed the States Reorganisation Commission in 1953, with Fazl Ali as its chairman and K. M. Panikkar and H. N. Kunzru as members.

The Commission examined demands for reorganising States. Language was an important consideration, but administrative, economic and national-integration concerns also mattered.

The States Reorganisation Act, 1956, together with related constitutional changes, produced a major redrawing of State boundaries on 1 November 1956.

The Mahagujarat Movement

Gujarati-speaking communities sought a separate State rather than continued inclusion in a larger bilingual Bombay State.

The Mahagujarat Movement became particularly prominent from 1956. It mobilised support around Gujarati linguistic and regional identity.

Indulal Yagnik was a prominent leader of the movement and was associated with the Mahagujarat Janata Parishad.

The movement demonstrated that linguistic identity could become the basis of democratic mobilisation for changing State boundaries.

Formation of Gujarat on 1 May 1960

Parliament enacted the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. The Act reorganised the bilingual Bombay State and provided for the creation of separate Gujarat and Maharashtra States.

Both States came into existence on 1 May 1960. This date is celebrated as Gujarat's State Formation Day.

The Act was enacted on 25 April 1960, but its appointed day for reorganisation was 1 May 1960. These 2 dates should not be confused.

The Dravidian movement and language politics

In southern India, the Dravidian movement developed around regional identity, social reform and opposition to perceived cultural and political domination.

E. V. Ramasamy, widely known as Periyar, was an important leader associated with anti-caste social reform and the Dravidar Kazhagam.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) subsequently emerged as an electoral political organisation. It participated in campaigns defending Tamil linguistic identity, including opposition to the compulsory or predominant use of Hindi.

Anti-Hindi agitations in 1965 increased support for the DMK. In the 1967 Madras Assembly election, the DMK came to power under C. N. Annadurai.

Hindi is an official language of the Union under Article 343. The Constitution does not declare Hindi to be India's national language. A question referring to official language and national language is testing 2 different concepts.

The Punjabi Suba movement

In northern India, demands for a Punjabi-speaking State were associated with the Punjabi Suba movement, in which the Akali Dal played an important role.

The Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966 reorganised the former Punjab. The present linguistic arrangement involving Punjab and Haryana emerged on 1 November 1966. Some hill areas were also transferred to Himachal Pradesh.

How does Parliament create or alter States?

Article 3 of the Constitution gives Parliament power to form new States and alter the areas, boundaries or names of existing States.

A Bill concerning such reorganisation requires the President's recommendation before introduction in Parliament. When an existing State is affected, the President refers the proposal to the State legislature for its views within a specified period. Parliament considers the proposal and may pass the law by a simple majority of members present and voting in each House; the affected State legislature's consent is not a constitutional requirement.

The law then goes to the President for assent. Thus, regional demands may initiate political discussion, but State formation is completed through a constitutional and legislative process.

Prelims focus

  • Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953.
  • The States Reorganisation Commission was chaired by Fazl Ali.
  • The States Reorganisation Act was enacted in 1956.
  • Gujarat and Maharashtra were formed on 1 May 1960.
  • Indulal Yagnik was associated with the Mahagujarat Movement.
  • Trap: Under Article 3, a State legislature's views are sought, but its consent is not mandatory.

[NCERT, Class 8, Our Pasts III, chapter 10, India After Independence, printed pp. 132–136; NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, chapter 8, Regional Aspirations, printed pp. 149–153 and 158–159; Directorate of Census Operations, Gujarat, Census of India 2011, District Census Handbook: Kheda, biographical entry on Indulal Yagnik; India Code, Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960, Sections 2 and 3; Ministry of Law and Justice, Constitution of India, Articles 3 and 343, edition as on 10 September 2026. Consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Linguistic Reorganisation and Regional Identity: Andhra, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Punjab
